chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Redman's five saxophones and three trombones
summary: Redman originated the five-saxophone and three-trombone sections; Jackson explains the voicings with Jerry Blake and Donald Kirkpatrick's arrangements, and lists the section.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: And going back to the band, of course, that's when we added the fifth saxophone because Don played alto, too.
And you tell me that's the first time that you heard any band use five saxophones. Is that right?
Just like he was the first one to have three trombones.
You never saw a band with three trombones before until -- ?
And then Don put five saxophones.
He also originated five sax, then?

That's right, he wrote for them and, of course, Donald Kirkpatrick, the piano player in the band, was a wonderful, wonderful arranger. He come in after Horace Henderson left. And he used to write for Chick Webb, too, and so he made a lot of arrangements for Don, beautiful arrangements. And sometimes Jerry Blake would play baritone. Other than that he'd play alto because we didn't use two tenors then. We used three altos. And then when Don would play alto, the lead alto, then Jerry Blake would play the tenor part, which would make five saxophones.

Sometimes he'd use a combination like soprano on top and the two altos and the tenor and the baritone. The baritone would play a lot of times what the bass clarinet would play today. They would write it that way, too, like sometimes there'd be soprano on top and then three clarinets, you see, and then the baritone on the bottom, and Jerry would play a kind of subtone effect so it would blend with the clarinets, you see.
And the soprano made a beautiful, beautiful sound.
: You know who the five -- Did you

Oh, I mentioned the three before. I mentioned Rupert Cole and Edward Inge on altos and Bob Carroll on tenor. And then we got Jerry Blake for the baritone, and he played alto, too, and played good solos and good clarinet, good clarinet. He was one of the most soulful clarinet players. Two good clarinet players in that band. Inge was a technician and then Jerry was really the [solo] man, actually, you would call it.

And, of course, we had -- Claude had left the band. Claude Jones had left the band and we got Gene Simon in the trombone section so we still had three trombones. And the same trumpet section, Sidney DeParis, Manzie Langston Curl, and Shirley Clay. And Manzie Johnson and --
Uh-huh, and Bobby Ysaguirre on bass.
